title: "Administrative quality control data as an oracle: verifying encoded SNAP rules and simulating payment error under cost sharing"
author:

    affiliations:
      - name: PolicyEngine
    email: max@policyengine.org
date: 2026-08-06
bibliography: references.bib
abstract: |
  Beginning in fiscal year 2028, each state's SNAP payment error rate sets its
  share of benefit costs, in steps of five percentage points at rates of 6, 8,
  and 10 percent. A measurement system built for program oversight now moves
  hundreds of millions of dollars per state per year, which raises two
  questions this paper treats as one: whether the rules that produce benefit
  amounts can be executed correctly, and how the errors that remain should be
  measured, modeled, and simulated. We use the USDA Quality Control public-use
  files as a verification oracle for independently encoded SNAP rules,
  reproducing 6,081 sampled case computations across seven states exactly, at
  zero tolerance, in six asserted stages per case — a process that surfaced
  and fixed two defects in our own encodings and errata in the federal
  technical documentation. We then decompose Colorado's fiscal 2024 error
  dollars by replaying reconstructed pre-edit case facts through the verified
  engine: 86.9% of filtered error cases are correct arithmetic on wrong facts.
  Building on that distinction, we fit and validate a distributional model of
  case-level payment deviations, and embed it in an open, in-browser Monte
  Carlo simulator of measured error rates under the new cost-sharing formula,
  where sampling noise alone gives several states nearly even odds of landing
  in a different cost tier than their point rate implies.
---

## Introduction

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act rewired the incentives around a statistic that
few people outside program-integrity offices had reason to watch. Under
7 U.S.C. 2013(a)(2), a state whose SNAP payment error rate reaches 6% will pay
5% of benefit costs from fiscal year 2028; at 8%, the share is 10%; at 10%, it
is 15%. The rate that determines the share is keyed to fiscal 2025 or 2026 at
the state's election, then to the third preceding year, and implementation is
delayed for the highest-error states — to FY2029 or FY2030 where 1.5 times the
keyed rate reaches 20%.[^delay] For a mid-sized state, one tier is worth tens
of millions of dollars a year; for the largest, hundreds of millions.

[^delay]: 7 U.S.C. 2013(a)(2)(B)(iii). The delay provision means the states
with the very highest measured rates face the formula later than everyone
else, a detail that matters for any projection of FY2028 outlays.

The error rate is estimated from the Quality Control (QC) system: each state
re-reviews a stratified sample of its own cases — on the order of hundreds to
a couple thousand active cases per year, set by formula in 7 C.F.R. 275.11 —
and federal reviewers re-review a subsample. The public-use files that result
[@fns2024techdoc] record, for roughly 45,000 cases a year, both what the
agency issued and what the reviewer concluded the case should have received,
along with the elements, natures, and causes of every discrepancy.

This paper treats those files as more than an audit byproduct. They are, we
argue, the best available *oracle* for executable encodings of SNAP rules:
tens of thousands of real, adjudicated benefit computations per year, each
carrying its inputs and its reviewed outputs. We use them three ways.

First, as a verification target. We test independently encoded SNAP rules —
statutes, regulations, and state manuals encoded as executable rule modules —
against every sampled case in seven states, and we hold the bar at exact
reproduction: zero dollar tolerance, six asserted computation stages per case
(@sec-oracle). Reaching that bar surfaced defects on three sides: two in our
own encodings, several in the federal technical documentation, and a class of
state-level computational discrepancies visible in the file itself.

Second, as the raw material for decomposing what "payment error" actually is.
QC's own cause coding, a finding-nature classification, and a replay of
reconstructed pre-edit case facts through the verified engine give three
nested estimates of how much of the error rate is computation — a rules-engine
failure — versus wrong facts faithfully processed (@sec-decompose). The
distinction determines what different interventions can plausibly buy.

Third, as training and validation data for a case-level model of the error
process (@sec-model), which powers a distributional simulator of measured
error rates under the OBBBA formula (@sec-simulate). The simulator, public at
[snap-qc-sim.vercel.app](https://snap-qc-sim.vercel.app), makes one point
vividly that summary statistics obscure: at regulatory sample sizes, the
measured rate is noisy enough that several states face nearly even odds of
being assigned a different cost tier than their point estimate implies.

Everything here is reproducible from public data. The analysis pipeline,
simulator, and this manuscript live in one repository;[^repo] the encoding
verification harness and its committed case-level reports are public; and the
pre-edit reconstruction builds on the open solver of @giannella_snapqc. Two
constraints we imposed on ourselves are worth stating up front, because they
shape the claims: every headline number in this paper survived an adversarial
audit that forced a full correction round of an earlier pipeline (targets,
universes, calibration protocol, and contrast construction all changed), and
every mechanism claim is scoped to what the artifacts show — including the
limits of our own parity result (@sec-oracle-scope).

[^repo]: github.com/PolicyEngine/snap-qc-sim. Analysis artifacts are
deterministic: two complete reruns of the pipeline produce byte-identical
outputs, independently reproduced by SHA-256 comparison.

## The QC system and the money attached to it {#sec-qc}

QC reviews produce, for each sampled case, the issued allotment, the
reviewer-determined correct allotment, and — when they differ by more than a
tolerance threshold ($56 in fiscal 2024) — a payment error with coded
findings. The official state rate is a regression-adjusted combination of
over- and underpayment rates estimated from these samples [@fns2024per].

Three features of the system matter for everything that follows.

**Sample sizes are set by formula and are small relative to the stakes.** The
active-case annual minimum is 300 for states with average monthly caseloads
up to 10,000, rising linearly (0.042 cases per additional unit) to a cap of
2,400; an optional reduced schedule — elected by every state in fiscal 2024
[@fns2024techdoc] — runs from 300 to a cap of 1,020. Colorado's fiscal 2024
edited file contains 856 active cases; the largest states contribute around
a thousand.

**The tolerance and the target moved.** The error threshold, indexed
annually, was $38 in 2017 and $56 in 2024; analyses that pool years must
apply each year's own threshold, and models that predict "error" must be
explicit that the label is an adjudicated, thresholded quantity — reviewer
status codes together with the error amount — not any benefit discrepancy.

**The dollars are new.** Before OBBBA, the error rate carried reputational
and (episodically) liability consequences. From FY2028 it prices directly:
applying the tier schedule to fiscal 2024 issuance, a state at Colorado's
position (official rate 9.97%, issuance $1.27B) has an expected annual cost
share of $156M with a standard deviation of $33M across sampling draws, and
the single step from the 10% to the 15% tier is worth about $63M per year
(@sec-simulate).

## The QC file as a verification oracle {#sec-oracle}

Rules-as-code — encoding statutes and regulations as executable, testable
logic — has a well-known validation problem: against what do you test the
encoding? Unit tests encode the encoder's own reading; cross-model
comparisons inherit both models' assumptions [@merigoux2021catala;
@oecd2020cracking]. Administrative QC data offers something stronger: real
cases, adjudicated by the agency's own reviewers, with inputs and outputs
recorded at case level.

We tested encodings of federal SNAP law and seven states' policy manuals
(Arizona, California, Colorado, Georgia, Maryland, New York, Texas),
maintained in the open rulespec-us repository and executed by a deterministic
rules engine, against every fiscal 2024 QC case in those states: 6,081 cases
in total (856 in Colorado; 847 New York; 883 California; 922 Arizona; 945
Georgia; 722 Maryland; 906 Texas). For each case the harness asserts six
values — gross income, standard deduction, excess shelter deduction, net
income, maximum allotment, and benefit — against the file's recorded values,
at zero dollar tolerance.

All 6,081 cases match on all asserted values: 36,486 exact cell comparisons
(5,136 in Colorado alone), no mismatches, no missing values, no engine
errors.

### What reaching exactness taught {#sec-oracle-findings}

The result is less interesting than the path to it. Early runs did not match,
and each mismatch class was a finding about somebody's rules:

- **Two defects in our own encodings.** A regulatory dollar literal that had
  been superseded by statute (the encoding faithfully reproduced a stale
  source), and a missing whole-dollar rounding step in the benefit chain.
  Both were fixed in the public encoding repository; the oracle is what
  caught them.
- **Errata in the federal technical documentation.** Mapping the file to
  engine inputs surfaced internal inconsistencies in the FY2024 technical
  documentation's variable descriptions, reported upstream. The oracle
  audits its own paperwork.
- **A residue that is not ours.** Once the encodings reproduce the reviewer
  arithmetic exactly, remaining discrepancies in *issued* amounts are
  attributable to the issuing side — the subject of @sec-decompose.

An audit process that treats mismatches as information, rather than noise to
be tolerated away, is the core of the method. We held tolerance at zero
precisely because a $1 tolerance would have hidden the rounding defect.

### Scope: what the parity result does and does not certify {#sec-oracle-scope}

Exactness claims invite overreading, so we state the scope precisely. The
comparison bridge supplies several intermediates directly from the QC file
rather than deriving them from raw case facts: the QC-calculated medical and
child-support deduction amounts, the recorded utility allowance amount, and
the recorded categorical-eligibility status. Parity therefore certifies that
the encoded *computation chain from those intermediates to the benefit* —
income aggregation, deduction sequencing, net-income arithmetic, allotment
lookup, and rounding — is exact on every sampled case. It does not certify
independent derivation of every state-specific eligibility and deduction
pathway from raw facts. Extending the bridge to feed raw facts (recorded
medical expenses rather than the computed deduction; energy-assistance facts
rather than the utility tier) is implemented as future work in the same
harness, and is the necessary next step before the engine can compute
counterfactual *intermediates* under alternative policy (@sec-roadmap).

### Certification as an artifact {#sec-cert}

Reproducibility claims should themselves be reproducible. We certified a
pinned toolchain — engine commit `de0efdc7` (binary SHA-256 `bb8ec236…`) with
encoding-repository commit `b53ce208` — by rebuilding offline and re-running
the full Colorado suite: 856/856 benefits and 5,136/5,136 stage cells, zero
tolerance, with every applied parameter-overlay file hash recorded. The run
takes 3.7 seconds end to end on a laptop (230 cases per second; 279/s with
compilation amortized), which extrapolates to about 26 seconds for the full
seven-state suite and roughly 16 minutes for a nationwide five-scenario
simulation batch. Verification at administrative scale is not a compute
problem.

## Decomposing measured error: computation versus facts {#sec-decompose}

If a verified engine issued every benefit, how much of the measured error
rate would disappear? The QC file supports three nested answers, from
generous to strict. We use Colorado fiscal 2024 as the worked example: 305 of
856 sampled cases carry payment errors, $112.6M per year in weighted error
dollars on $1.268B of issuance (the file-derived 8.88%; the official
regression-adjusted rate is 9.97%).

**Layer 1 — QC's own cause codes.** Findings carry agency-cause codes.
Classes that name the computing apparatus — computer programming, arithmetic,
mass-change processing — account for $8.2M per year, 7.3% of Colorado's error
dollars; adding policy-misapplied, budgeted-wrong, and computer-user classes
reaches $11.9M (10.5%). Nationally the same coding yields $320M per year
(3.9%) strict and $1.5B (18.4%) broad, of $8.1B in weighted error dollars.

**Layer 2 — finding natures.** Classifying findings by *nature* (rounding,
income conversion, averaging, wrong standard, benefit incorrectly computed,
allotment-table, proration) with cause codes disambiguating deduction-amount
natures: pure-computation cases carry 3.3% of error dollars,
system-caused-input cases 6.6%, mixed cases 4.2%, and other input errors
86.0%.

**Layer 3 — engine replay.** The strictest test reconstructs each error
case's pre-edit original values using the public $3-shift reconstruction
solver [@giannella_snapqc], adapted to fiscal 2024, then replays those
original facts through the verified engine and compares to what the agency
actually issued. Of 283 error cases surviving the solver's consistency
filters, 246 — 86.9% — reproduce the issued amount: the agency's arithmetic
was correct, applied to wrong facts. The solver and the engine partition the
283 cases identically, an independent cross-validation of both. The residual
37 cases are the upper bound on computation-side failure observable this way;
they include solver limitations as well as genuine multi-variable or
computational discrepancies.

The three layers agree on the structure: **the large majority of SNAP payment
error is information failure, not calculation failure.** Correct-computation
guarantees — the thing a verified rules engine directly provides — address
the smaller share directly (roughly 3–10% of error dollars by layers 1–2, and
bounded above by 13.1% in the replay), plus whatever share of
information failures better tooling prevents indirectly (verification
prompts, documentation-requirement computation, consistency checks at
intake). That indirect channel is exactly where policy *design* enters: rules
determine how much information a caseworker must collect and verify, which is
the mechanism the modeling section takes up.

## Modeling the error process {#sec-model}

Decomposition is retrospective. Pricing decisions — how much a documentation
requirement costs in error, what an audit-volume change buys — require a
model of the error-generating process at case level. We fit one on the QC
files for 2017–2019 and 2022–2023 (pandemic years excluded), evaluating on
fiscal 2024: 217,656 training and 44,800 evaluation cases in the official
`CASE == 1` universe, all estimates weighted by the file's case weights.

Targets are defined from the file's own adjudication fields. The official
error label is reviewer status (over- or underpayment) with an error amount
above the year's threshold. The signed deviation is issued minus corrected
allotment (`RAWBEN − BENFIX`), which reconciles with the recorded error
amount for 99.997% of weighted fiscal 2024 cases; the full recomputed benefit
(`FSBEN`) — an earlier, wrong choice of target that an adversarial audit
caught — matches only 83.65%, because it conflates legitimate adjustments
such as proration with error.[^audit]

[^audit]: The correction round replaced targets, enforced the official case
universe, rebuilt features whose source columns had been silently missing,
scanned all nine finding slots rather than three, and replaced an in-sample
state calibration with the temporal protocol described below. We document
this because the corrected numbers differ materially from what the
uncorrected pipeline produced, and because the audit-and-correct loop is, in
our view, as much a part of the method as the models.

**Discrimination.** A gradient-boosted classifier on household covariates
plus a formula-benefit anchor reaches weighted ROC AUC 0.761 on fiscal 2024;
adding policy-burden intermediates extracted from the file (medical-expense
claiming and documentation-requirement proxies, self-employment records,
utility-claim structure, deduction counts) moves it to 0.767 (+0.006 AUC,
+0.003 PR-AUC). The honest statement is that burden intermediates add little
*discrimination* on this label. Operationally the model is nonetheless
useful: at a 5% weighted review budget it reaches 47.8% precision against a
13.4% base rate — case targeting at three and a half times chance.

**The deviation distribution.** For simulation we need more than a
probability: a per-case distribution of the signed deviation. A hurdle
structure estimates P(any deviation) (AUC 0.836) and P(above-threshold |
deviation) (AUC 0.723), both isotonic-calibrated out of fold; a sign model
(calibrated AUC 0.700); and nine conditional quantiles of log |D| fitted by
quantile-loss gradient boosting [@koenker1978quantile], made monotone per
case, with an exponential-in-logs tail beyond the 99th percentile fitted on
top-decile out-of-fold residuals (scale 0.467, satisfying the finite-mean
condition). Conditional magnitudes retransform with an out-of-fold Duan
smear of 1.173 [@duan1983smearing]; predicted mean conditional magnitude is
$183 against $189 observed.

**Validation.** Weighted quantile coverage on fiscal 2024 deviators is
within 3 percentage points of nominal at seven of nine levels (the 75th and
90th percentiles over-cover by 3.5 and 3.3 points — the model slightly
overstates mid-upper magnitudes). State-level calibration uses a strictly
temporal protocol: models fit through 2022 predict 2023 out of sample; state
observed-to-predicted ratios, shrunk by an empirical-Bayes precision rule,
are frozen and applied to fiscal 2024. Unfactored, state mean absolute error
is 1.83 points (equal-weighted) and 1.45 (issuance-weighted); with the
frozen 2023 factors, 0.885 and 0.785 points, with cross-state correlation
0.906. We report the unfactored numbers alongside because the factors absorb
persistent state-level residuals whose interpretation — administration,
omitted policy, model error — the data do not identify.

One validation failure is worth featuring rather than burying: simulated at
its raw level, the model underpredicts high-error states (New York's
simulated mean measured rate is 11.0% against a 14.1% observed-bootstrap
mean). Per-case features carry within-state structure but only part of the
cross-state level differences. The simulator therefore anchors each state's
baseline at its official rate and uses the model for distribution shape and
within-state heterogeneity, an anchoring choice stated in the tool.

**Policy contrasts are descriptive.** States that operate a standard medical
deduction show slightly *lower* medical-error event rates in cross-section
(2.60% versus 2.97% among elderly/disabled claimants, under an event
definition requiring a medical finding with payment impact); but adoption is
endogenous, and calendar-aligned adoption contrasts against never-adopting
states are small and mixed (Arizona +2.07 points claimant-conditioned but
+0.64 on the stable denominator; Kentucky −0.42 claimant-conditioned;
California, Louisiana, Michigan near zero), with single-digit event counts
for several adopters. An earlier pipeline's dramatic Kentucky estimate
(−5.3 points) dissolved under the corrected event definition and windows —
a caution we pass on. Causal identification of burden-policy effects on
error awaits the engine-computed counterfactuals of @sec-roadmap.

## Simulating measured rates under cost sharing {#sec-simulate}

The public simulator wraps two Monte Carlo modes around the QC file.

**Observed resample.** Each draw resamples the state's own sampled cases
with replacement at the realized (or a hypothetical, larger) sample size and
recomputes the weighted error rate [@efron1979bootstrap], centered on the
official rate. This mode makes no modeling assumptions beyond the sample
representing the state's case mix.

**Model-based.** Each draw additionally re-draws every sampled case's
deviation from its fitted distribution (@sec-model), executed in the browser
by inverting the exported quantile function — so the measured rate varies
both because the sample composition varies and because each case's error
realization varies. Baselines anchor at the official rate as described
above; the mode's mechanism and its distinction from the observed resample
are labeled in the interface.

Three findings from the simulator, all on fiscal 2024 data:

**Tier assignment is a coin flip for boundary states.** With no policy
change at all, the probability that a fresh QC-style sample lands in a
different cost-share tier than the official point rate implies is 49% for
North Dakota (official rate 7.91%), 48% for Washington (6.06%), 47% for
Colorado (9.97%), Kansas (9.98%), and Nevada (5.94%). The formula prices a
noisy estimate as if it were the truth; near a boundary, sampling noise is
worth more than most feasible policy improvements.

**Audit volume is a two-sided instrument.** Increasing the QC sample size
shrinks sampling variance around the state's underlying rate. In
expectation that *helps* states sitting just below a boundary — the tighter
distribution protects the better tier (Missouri +$4.0M, Tennessee +$3.7M,
Indiana +$3.3M expected annual savings from 500 additional reviews) — and
*hurts* states just above one, for whom variance was a lottery ticket
(California −$29.5M, Pennsylvania −$13.3M, Texas −$13.2M in expectation).
Yet added volume almost always reduces the standard deviation of the annual
bill (California by $43M), so risk-averse states may rationally buy audits
even against their expectation. The formula thus embeds an incentive
asymmetry: below-boundary states are rewarded for measuring more precisely;
above-boundary states are rewarded for preserving noise.

**Simplification levers carry large accounting bounds.** Suppressing the
observed error dollars attached to the finding elements that four policy
options standardize — the standard medical deduction, standard
self-employment deduction, heat-and-eat utility standardization, and
broad-based categorical eligibility resource exemptions — is worth roughly
$606M per year nationally in expected cost share at 50% effectiveness, and
$1.31B at 100%. We label these *accounting bounds*, not causal estimates:
they hold the error process fixed and answer "what if these categories'
observed error dollars shrank," which is an upper-bound identity, not a
behavioral prediction. The descriptive adoption contrasts of @sec-model are
the reason for the caution. Deep-in-tier states get little from marginal
simplification (New York at 14.1% and Alaska at 24.7% need larger moves);
boundary states get the most.

## From accounting bounds to engine-computed counterfactuals {#sec-roadmap}

The gap this paper leaves open is the one that matters most for policy
design: replacing accounting bounds with case-level counterfactuals in which
the *rules engine* recomputes both the correct benefit and the
policy-burden intermediates under alternative policy, and the error model
responds through those intermediates. The pieces now exist separately. The
toolchain is certified and fast (@sec-cert); the harness has a
parameter-overlay mechanism that already applies fiscal-year parameter
patches under recorded provenance; the model consumes burden intermediates
(@sec-model). The work between is precise and bounded: feeding the bridge
raw facts instead of QC-derived intermediates (@sec-oracle-scope), so that
recomputed intermediates can *differ* under counterfactual policy; encoding
the "off" state of options whose current encodings are structural rather
than scalar; and defining scenario semantics for states without the option.
Self-employment counterfactuals face a data constraint — the public file
records net rather than gross self-employment income — that engine work
cannot remove.

We also note the encoding target the cost-sharing formula itself deserves:
the QC sampling formulas of 7 C.F.R. 275.11(b) and the tier schedule of
7 U.S.C. 2013(a)(2), including its election and delay clauses, are
themselves rules that can be encoded, tested at their published boundary
values, and cited by simulators, replacing hand-transcribed constants.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

The parity result certifies computation from QC-derived intermediates, not
full-path derivation (@sec-oracle-scope). The replay decomposition depends
on a reconstruction solver whose filters exclude 22 of 305 error cases and
whose residual class is an upper bound, not a point estimate. The error
models predict an adjudicated, thresholded label — properties of the QC
measurement system, not just of underlying payment accuracy; a state whose
reviewers find errors differently is a different measurement regime.
Cross-state model transport is imperfect (the New York level gap), which is
why the simulator anchors at official rates. All simulation results hold
the error process fixed: no behavioral response of agencies or households
to cost sharing, no corrective-feedback channel from audit volume, both of
which are live questions the fiscal 2025–2027 files will begin to answer.
Adoption contrasts are descriptive; nothing here identifies causal effects
of burden policies on error. And the model-based simulator mode currently
covers baseline and audit-volume scenarios only; policy levers remain
accounting bounds until the counterfactual leg lands.

## Conclusion

A measurement system designed for oversight now sets prices. That makes the
QC files three things at once: the highest-value verification oracle
available to rules-as-code work in the benefits space; the dataset that
shows most measured error to be information failure rather than computation
failure; and the sampling frame whose noise the new formula converts into
tier lotteries for boundary states. The verification bar can be exact —
6,081 cases, six stages, zero tolerance — and holding it there is what makes
the residuals informative. The modeling bar cannot be exact, and we have
tried to be as clear about what the models miss as what they capture. Both
kinds of honesty are prerequisites for the system this points toward: one
in which the rules that compute benefits, the requirements they impose on
households, and the errors they produce are all executable, testable, and
priced from the same verified source.

## Reproducibility

The repository `PolicyEngine/snap-qc-sim` contains the analysis pipeline
(deterministic; two complete reruns byte-identical, independently
reproduced by SHA-256), the simulator, frozen simulation and certification
artifacts under `paper/snapshot/`, and this manuscript. The verification
harness, per-case suite reports, and encodings are public in
`TheAxiomFoundation/axiom-oracles` and `TheAxiomFoundation/rulespec-us`.
QC public-use files are available from USDA FNS [@fns2024techdoc]. The
pre-edit reconstruction solver is @giannella_snapqc. A fact catalog mapping
every quantitative claim in this manuscript to its artifact is committed
alongside it (`paper/FACTS.md`).
